 The sunset silhouettes the gazebo at Pleasant Lake northeast of Fairfield on Wednesday evening. The 114-acre park around the lake offers walking trails and a boat ramp. The park is managed by Jefferson County Conservation. With the end of daylight saving time, the sun now sets around 4:50 p.m. (Jim Slosiarek/The Gazette)
 JIM SLOSIAREK 
 With Congress once again considering the Sunshine Protection Act, lawmakers may finally do something most Americans can agree upon: end the twice-yearly changing of clocks.
 Americans are understandably tired of springing forward and falling back. But as Congress revisits the issue, an important distinction is being overlooked: ending clock changes and adopting permanent daylight saving time are not the same thing.
 The real question is not whether we should stop changing our clocks. Most Americans seem ready to do that. The better question is this: Which permanent time standard best serves human flourishing? That question matters especially in Iowa.
 We understand winter darkness. We know the quiet of a January morning before the sun has fully considered rising, the crunch of snow beneath our boots, and the glow of headlights stretching across rural roads before dawn. In Iowa, morning light is not merely pleasant. It is precious.
 Advocates of permanent daylight saving time point to brighter evenings, and understandably so. Most of us enjoy an extra hour of daylight after work. Yet every public policy involves tradeoffs. The brighter evenings of permanent DST would come at the cost of darker winter mornings, pushing sunrise toward 9:00 A.M. across much of the Midwest.
 We have tried this before.
 During the energy crisis of the 1970s, the nation experimented with year-round daylight saving time. Public support quickly eroded as concerns arose over children waiting for school buses in darkness, workers commuting before dawn, and communities struggling to adjust to mornings that seemed disconnected from the natural day. Congress eventually reversed course.
 The lessons of that experiment remain relevant. Iowa is still a rural state. Children still wait for buses before sunrise. Farmers, factory workers, health-care professionals and countless others still begin their days long before many office lights come on.
 What has changed is our understanding of human health. Researchers increasingly recognize the importance of morning light in regulating sleep patterns, supporting mental health, improving alertness, and helping our bodies maintain healthy circadian rhythms. Human beings do not simply keep time. We respond to light. The rising sun remains one of the most important signals our bodies receive.
 It is no surprise, then, that many sleep researchers and medical experts have concluded that permanent standard time aligns more closely with natural human biology than permanent daylight saving time. In other words, the time standard that most closely reflects the movement of the sun is also the one most consistent with human health. As a pastor, I find that conclusion unsurprising.
 Scripture begins with light. Before anything else, God speaks: "Let there be light." Throughout the biblical story, morning carries special significance. Manna appears with the morning dew. The women arrive at Christ's tomb at dawn. The prophet reminds us that God's mercies are "new every morning."
 These images endure because they speak to something deeply human. Morning light steadies us. It orients us. It reminds us that each day begins not in darkness but in hope.
 This is not merely a religious observation. It is a recognition that human flourishing is connected to the created order. We are creatures, not machines. When public policy works with the rhythms woven into creation, communities tend to flourish. When it works against them, unintended consequences often follow.
 This is not a partisan argument. It is a pastoral one.
 As a pastor, I have walked with families grieving accidents on rural roads. I have listened to exhausted shift workers describe the struggle of living out of sync with healthy sleep patterns. I have heard teachers speak about students trying to learn when their day begins in darkness.
 The desire to end clock changes is understandable. On that point, Congress and the American people largely agree.
 But if lawmakers are finally prepared to choose one permanent time standard, they should choose the one that best serves children waiting at bus stops, workers beginning early shifts, rural communities navigating winter mornings, and families seeking healthier daily rhythms.
 Congress has identified the right problem. Now it must avoid embracing the wrong solution.
 Permanent standard time may not promise brighter evenings, but it offers something even more valuable: a society more closely aligned with the rhythms of light, safety, health and human flourishing.
 The Rev. Neil P. Harrison is senior pastor of First Lutheran Church in Maquoketa and a former Iowa legislator.
